This bill would authorise spending from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for government services that are not part of its ordinary annual services.
It is one of three Additional Estimates Appropriation Bills for the 2025-2026 financial year, alongside the Appropriation Bill (No. 3) and the Appropriation (Parliamentary Departments) Bill (No. 2).
The appropriations cover government decisions made since the 2025-26 Budget, and details are in the Portfolio Additional Estimates Statements.
Proposes appropriations from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for non-ordinary annual services.
Forms part of the Additional Estimates Appropriation Bills for 2025-2026.
Provides funding for government decisions made after the 2025-26 Budget.
The Australian Government and its agencies.

Andrew Bragg I rise to make a contribution in relation to the Appropriation Bill (No. 3) 2025-2026, Appropriation Bill (No. 4) 2025-2026 and Appropriation (Parliamentary Departments) Bill (No. 2) 2025-2026. The main point to make is that the nation's finances are no longer within the control of the government. We are now looking at a situation of an almost $40 billion deficit this year and a well over $100 billion deficit over the forward estimates. The reality is that public finances in Australia are completely broken. They're completely broken because the government has decided that it wants to spend at beyond pandemic levels on an ongoing basis—at 27 per cent of GDP—and, as a result, it has needed to find new tax revenues. The other point to make is that the government has completely debased the integrity of public finances with its commitment to significant off-budget funding. When you look at the overall position of the Commonwealth government, we can talk about the deficit, we can talk about the structural deficit, we can talk about the spending and we can talk about the overreliance on a small number—a shrinking number—of Australians for the tax base. But I think one of the biggest problems is this issue of integrity. This government has sought to provide all sorts of different boondoggle funds, like the Future Made in Australia fund, the housing fund, the rewiring fund and the reconstruction fund—I'm still not sure what we're reconstructing from—but all of these funds are off budget. None of them come into the main picture when the Treasurer hands down the budget. It's a pretty sad state of affairs when, at one level, you look at the budget deficit and you think, that's a pretty bad position—$40 billion this year, $100 billion over the forwards, at least, and we're approaching $1 trillion in debt. Moved the 2025-26 additional estimates appropriation bills, including Appropriation Bill (No. 3) 2025-2026, which seeks $9.2 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for measures and program variations in the 2025-26 financial year. Debate was adjourned.

Moved Appropriation Bill (No. 4) 2025-26, seeking $3.5 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for the 2025-26 financial year, including funding for Defence, water purchases under the Murray-Darling Basin Plan and Housing Australia loans. Debate was adjourned.

Tabled additional expenditure documents for the year ending on 30 June 2026 and moved that they, together with the final budget outcome 2024-25, be referred to committees for examination and report; the question was agreed to.

Referred Appropriation Bills No.3 and No.4 2025-2026 and the Appropriation (Parliamentary Departments) Bill No.2 2025-2026 to the Federation Chamber immediately, with two other bills to follow the adjournment of their second-reading debates.

Supported additional estimates appropriations for 2025-2026, outlining funding for cheaper home batteries, Medicare, medicines, mental health, community language schools, housing, first home buyers and training. Reported local initiatives and figures including 250,000 batteries installed, $25 PBS scripts, more than 21,000 new social and affordable homes, and $325 million for Housing Australia loans.

Argued that Australia's public finances were unsustainable, citing a deficit of almost $40 billion, more than $100 billion over the forward estimates and spending at 27 per cent of GDP. Criticised off-budget funds, high taxes and inadequate supply-side reform, and foreshadowed an amendment to remove funding for net zero measures before the bills' consideration continued.
